So, how do we harness these two seemingly separate but, in reality, interconnected and intertwined revolutions - the energy transition, and the AI era? This is the focus of our new Bulletin, below, where we define the ‘digital energy stack’.

In the tech world, a ’stack’ is the collection of different technologies and components needed for a digital product or service to function. As you read this post, it sits on a ’stack’ of solutions: a web browser or LinkedIn application on your phone or other device. Internet and email protocols that (hopefully!) are displaying the below graphic and link correctly. And, layers of cloud hosting, connectivity, and - of course - energy, to make all of this happen.

We are applying this ‘stack’ approach to sustainable energy. We need a systems-level approach, and coherent and strategic efforts. There are seven elements in the ’digital energy stack’:

📊 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 - the 'fuel' of the energy revolution. Big, Lean, and Thick Data.
📱 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 - including 3G and 4G, and IoT.
🖥️ 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐞 - the 'currency' of the 21st century.
🪪 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 - to amplify the impact of inclusive energy.
🔒 𝐂𝐲𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 - recognising energy's status as critical national infrastructure. 
🤖 𝐀𝐈 - with AI driving new energy solutions, but also creating new challenges.
🏛️ 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 - shaping the talent, culture, and  institutions of the energy transition.

Importantly, there is no single pathway for any of these seven components. Digital and energy innovation is occurring and emerging everywhere, from Silicon Valley to the Silicon Savannah. The Global South is not just an innovation taker - but a maker, and shaper.

Without intentional design, digital risks reinforcing and entrenching energy inequality rather than accelerating an inclusive and just energy transition. The question is no longer whether AI and energy will intersect. It is whether we design that intersection to deliver development, resilience, and equity at scale.

The #EnergyTransition is often discussed as a question of technology. The new #IRENA Innovation Landscape report makes clear that this framing is incomplete. The real bottleneck is not #Innovation itself, but how selectively and unevenly it is deployed. 

According to International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), renewable energy capacity must triple by 2030 to stay on a 1.5°C pathway. Yet today, over 75 percent of global clean energy investment is concentrated in a small group of countries, while many emerging and developing economies remain largely excluded from innovation-driven progress. At the same time, power systems are becoming more complex: higher shares of variable renewables, rising electrification, and growing digitalisation are stressing grids that were never designed for this role.

The status quo is therefore insufficient. Scaling renewables without parallel innovation in system design, markets, and institutions risks higher costs, social resistance, and missed development benefits. Technology alone will not deliver a just and resilient transition.

These gaps were also a central theme at the IRENA Youth Forum, where I discussed how innovation must translate into real-world development outcomes with my peers. In exchanges with practitioners, including Riad Meddeb from UNDP, one message stood out clearly: innovation only matters if it strengthens institutions, delivery capacity, and inclusion on the ground.

The report highlights three priorities that deserve far more policy attention:

1️⃣ System-level innovation must be treated as core infrastructure. Solutions such as advanced grid management, flexibility markets, storage, and sector coupling are not add-ons. They are prerequisites for high-renewables systems to function reliably at scale.

2️⃣ Innovation policy needs to shift from pilots to deployment. Many solutions already exist but remain stuck in demonstration phases. Clear regulation, bankable market frameworks, and public risk-sharing are essential to move from experimentation to impact.

3️⃣ Inclusiveness is an innovation challenge, not a side issue. Local value creation, skills development, and access to finance determine whether innovation strengthens energy security and development or deepens global inequalities.

The deeper message of the IRENA report is that innovation is a governance question. Who benefits, who decides, and who bears risk will shape the long-term legitimacy of the energy transition as much as cost curves or efficiency gains. Aligning innovation with equity and implementation capacity is no longer optional if the transition is to succeed at global scale. 

How do you see the balance between technological innovation and institutional reform in your own energy system context?

The 'Smart City' has been closely linked with #energy since the term was introduced. From smart energy meters, to the role of Big Data for energy and grid management. I've been getting more and more questions about what a 'smart' city looks like and wanted to re-share this article I co-authored with Calum Handforth a while back. We argue that we need fewer 'smart' cities, and more 'smarter' cities. Smarter cities which:

* Put people at the heart of urban and technology planning and deployment. Not cities that try to retro-fit tech and energy projects and programmes around perceived citizen needs.
* Use a broad tech and innovation toolkit, and don’t just chase the latest innovation. For example, Big Data is important, but so too is the 'Thick Data' which helps us to learn more about energy consumers - or those that are energy-poor.
* Focus on outcomes, and not just the rollout of solutions - and, especially, we need ‘Smarter Cities’ which invest in the ‘connective tissue’ that creates meaningful urban spaces and places. We don’t want cities to just become ‘platforms’ of ‘use-cases’.

When writing this article, we were also inspired by the exciting and important opportunities for 'smart cities' in the Global North to learn from their counterparts in the Global South. 

And this is particularly relevant for energy, when so many innovations - including decentralised renewable energy, pay-as-you-go solar and other innovative business models, and frugal energy innovations - could be as relevant in New York as they are in New Delhi.

Clean Energy in the Age of Data and AI: How Data and AI Are Reshaping Clean Energy and Development?

26 January marks the International Day of Clean Energy, a moment to reflect on how we deliver equitable and sustainable energy transitions that leave no one behind and protect our planet.

For every generation, energy progress has never been just about technology—it has been about expanding what people and societies are able to do. Steam turned heat into motion and powered the first industrial surge. Electricity multiplied development, bringing light to homes, power to industry, and refrigeration that keeps food and vaccines safe. Today, clean energy is becoming the backbone of a new development era—one increasingly shaped not only by electrons, but by data and artificial intelligence.

AI-enabled forecasting and optimisation can unlock up to 175 GW of additional transmission capacity without building new lines, delivering power to millions of people. In practice, better forecasting has already increased wind power value by up to 20% and reduced outage duration by as much as half in some systems.

But this impact is not automatic. Without deliberate design and governance, data and AI can deepen strain on energy systems. When used intentionally, they can strengthen access, resilience, and fairness, and help deliver a just energy transition.

So how do we maximise these gains without creating or entrenching a new digital and energy divide?

1️⃣ Energy data must be treated as public infrastructure
Open, trusted data on demand, grid capacity, and system performance reduces uncertainty and unlocks investment at scale. When data is shared, the benefits of AI and digital tools can move from pilots to systems.

2️⃣ AI and energy must operate within land, water, and social limits
Efficiency gains matter only if they respect resource constraints and local realities. Digital optimisation cannot come at the expense of people or ecosystems.

3️⃣ Al needs to deliver for people
The growth of energy, digital, and AI should be judged by whether intelligence expands access, resilience, and livelihoods, not just system performance.
The opportunities are real. Data and AI can accelerate the energy transition in ways we have never seen before. 

But only if they are governed deliberately, aligned with development goals, and designed to serve people first.

#InternationalDayOfCleanEnergy #CleanEnergyDay #AI

Celebrating the International Clean Energy Day by following the discussions at the ECOSOC Partnership Forum 2026, where UNDP , World Meteorological Organization (WMO), and UNECE-UN/CEFACT explored the digital–energy nexus at a defining moment for global development.
The panel featuring Dr. Latifa Yousef, PhD , Mr. Albert Williams , Dr. Elizabeth Massey , Prof. Brian Min , Mr. Riad Meddeb , and Prof. Amir Lebdioui , offered a timely and thoughtful conversation on how digitalization and energy systems must evolve together to support inclusive, resilient development.
One intervention that strongly resonated with me was from Mr. Meddeb, He reminded us that every major technological breakthrough in history - from steam power to electrification - has been underwritten by an energy transition. AI, he noted, is simply the next wave, but its impact will not be determined by algorithms alone.
His key message was clear:
The real test of AI lies in whether energy systems and digital infrastructure evolve together; at speed, at scale, and in ways that expand access, affordability, and opportunity, especially for the Global South.
Mr. Meddeb emphasized four critical points:
● Affordability and risk management are where the energy transition will ultimately succeed or fail, particularly for the 1.18 billion people still living in energy poverty.
● High-quality, trusted, interoperable data - not just more data - is essential for managing risk, stabilizing costs, and improving utility performance.
● Governance and digital public infrastructure are as important as AI adoption itself, enabling countries to move from being users of technology to shapers of it.
● People and skills matter as much as platforms, with sustained investment needed across engineers, regulators, utilities, communities, and consumers.
Above all, his closing reminder stood out:
Energy is not an end in itself, it is a means to improve lives.
Whether a clinic can refrigerate vaccines, a school can connect to the world, or a small business can grow, this is the true measure of the digital energy transition.
A powerful and grounding conversation that reinforced why energy, digitalization, and development must be pursued as one integrated agenda. #ECOSOC #InternationalCleanEnergyDay #UNDP #EnergyAccess #DigitalTransformation #AIforGood #CleanEnergy #GlobalDevelopment #EnergyTransition

Everyone loves handing out/receiving carrots in climate and green industrial policy, but few politicians want to talk about the sticks, which are more politically sensitive.

A new important paper in Nature by Wei Peng, Jonas Meckling, Huilin Luo, Allen Fawcett, Jonas Nahm Jessica F. Green, Gokul Iyer, & David G. Victor explores what happens to decarbonisation when we sequence carrots (e.g. green subsidies) and sticks (carbon taxes).

They find that carrots alone (without shifting to sticks) does not achieve deep decarbonization by mid-century, and you still need almost the same size sticks later anyway. In other words, sequencing matters but cannot substitute for the presence and quality of sticks. Delaying hard policies does not necessarily avoids them; it may just postpones them, potentially at higher cost.

The next question: what types of sticks are more likely to be effective than others, under what conditions and for different objectives, such as green industrial capability accumulation in developing nations?

Article:  https://lnkd.in/eNzEyjk6. 

Center for Policy Research on Energy and the Environment, Princeton University, New Energy Industrial Strategy (NEIS) Center

Since independence, Gara Djebilet, one of the world’s largest untapped iron ore deposits, captivated imaginations but was deemed too remote, too logistically complex. 3. Green.Green.Green . Algeria CAN and SHOULD become a major green steel player if energy integration is smart. There has a market premium for greener steel production! Using fossil-fuel based electricity for transforming this iron ore will be a missed opportunity.  

4. The success of the project to date is also a testament to the efficiency of south-south cooperation and particularly Chinese technical prowess, not just at home but also abroad.

Digitalisation of energy systems is not just a technical pathway. It is a development choice. It shapes energy reliability for households, competitiveness for industries, and fiscal efficiency for states.

AI and advanced digital tools can already reduce technical and commercial losses by 10–30%, improve grid flexibility, and accelerate the integration of variable renewables through forecasting, demand response, and predictive maintenance. But scale changes the equation. 

As digital infrastructure expands: how do we grow an already energy-intensive digital sector in a way that is efficient, fair, and sustainable?

The stakes are real. In South Asia, low-income households spend over 10% of their income on basic energy services, while grid losses reach 17–20%. At the same time, data centres are projected to consume around 945 TWh of electricity by 2030, with significant water demands.

Three priorities help reframe the challenge:

🏭 Treat digital loads as industrial policy
Clean, flexible power systems are needed to support energy-intensive digital infrastructure without locking in new emissions.

♻️ Turn digital footprints into community benefits
Clean energy supply for AI should be guided by system-level planning, not narrow self-sufficiency approaches. When integrated into power and urban systems, digital infrastructure can anchor new renewable capacity, enable waste-heat recovery and circular energy use, and support the wider electrification of transport, industry, and surrounding communities.

🌍 Use planetary intelligence as a guiding framework
AI can help interpret and protect ecological limits, supporting digital systems that work with planetary boundaries, not against them.

Digital acceleration strengthens development only when built on renewable, reliable, and affordable energy systems. The real question is not whether AI and energy will intersect, but how we design that intersection to deliver equity and resilience at scale.

Global electricity demand is projected to grow by 3.6% annually between 2026 and 2030, driven by industry, electric mobility, cooling and data centres. Emerging economies will account for nearly 80% of additional demand, placing the Global South at the centre of this transformation. At the same time, renewables are set to overtake coal, with renewables and nuclear reaching 50% of global generation by 2030, up from 42% today, while solar and wind rise from 17% to 27%. This shift creates a historic opportunity to align energy expansion with development and industrial transformation. 

Yet affordability remains a critical constraint, as electricity prices in many countries have risen faster than incomes since 2019. The pathway forward lies in designing power systems that deliver efficiency across demand, supply and infrastructure use—through smart grids, regional interconnections, demand-side management, and blended finance mechanisms that crowd in private capital while protecting vulnerable households.

Unlocking these opportunities requires three interconnected solutions:

1. Scale grids and storage at speed. Annual grid investment must increase by roughly 50% from today’s USD 400 billion, combined with accelerated deployment of utility-scale batteries to enhance flexibility and energy security.

2. Develop integrated, development-focused energy systems. Combining grid expansion, distributed renewables, storage and digital system management can support electrification of transport, industry and communities while reducing import dependence.

3. Ensure affordability and financial sustainability. Smart market design, demand-side efficiency, regional interconnections and blended finance mechanisms can crowd in private capital, protect vulnerable households and stabilize prices.

With global power sector emissions plateauing through 2030, the just energy transition is no longer a future aspiration—it is a present reality. The Global South is already demonstrating leadership in renewable expansion and system innovation, proving that development and decarbonization can advance together, and setting the pace for a more resilient and inclusive global energy system in our societies.

How can countries leverage green hydrogen to decarbonize hard-to-electrify industries while strengthening development outcomes?

Global hydrogen demand reached 100 million tonnes (Mt) in 2024, growing by nearly 2% from 2023, in line with overall energy demand growth. Yet it is still produced almost entirely from fossil fuels, consuming around 290 billion cubic metres of natural gas and 90 million tonnes of coal equivalent each year. The transition to low-emissions hydrogen is therefore not marginal — it is systemic.

For emerging and developing economies, this transition represents a strategic development opportunity.

Hard-to-electrify sectors such as steel, chemicals, refining, shipping and aviation will require energy-dense, low-carbon fuels. If designed well, green hydrogen can reduce exposure to fossil fuel volatility, strengthen energy security, create skilled jobs and anchor new industrial value chains —when guided by strong governance and development-focused strategies.

Our report identifies three priorities to ensure green hydrogen supports equitable development:

⚖️ Build strategic foundations before committing to scale
With global hydrogen demand still dominated by fossil-based supply and costs for low-emissions hydrogen remaining 2–4 times higher in many regions, countries should prioritize phased pilots. Strategic demonstration projects allow learning, cost discovery, and institutional strengthening without creating fiscal or technological lock-in.

🔗 Integrate green hydrogen into broader industrial policy
Hydrogen should not be treated as a standalone sector. It must be embedded in coordinated energy planning, renewable capacity expansion, infrastructure development, skills strategies, and industrial upgrading. Given that hydrogen production requires large volumes of additional renewable electricity, system-level planning is essential to avoid diverting clean power away from households and productive sectors.

💰 De-risk strategically with governance safeguards
Blended finance, carbon contracts for difference, and public guarantees can help close viability gaps and crowd in private capital. But de-risking must be conditional on environmental safeguards, renewable additionality, water sustainability, local job creation, and transparent revenue frameworks to ensure that hydrogen projects contribute to long-term development outcomes.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these principles into practical strategies—supporting hydrogen roadmaps, identifying bankable projects, and aligning development with jobs, skills, environmental safeguards, and local industrial priorities.

For sectors where direct electrification is not feasible, green hydrogen can provide a pathway toward net-zero when aligned with inclusive development goals.

Global hydrogen demand reached 100 million tonnes (Mt) in 2024, growing by nearly 2% from 2023, in line with overall energy demand growth. Yet it is still produced almost entirely from fossil fuels, consuming around 290 billion cubic metres of natural gas and 90 million tonnes of coal equivalent each year. The transition to low-emissions hydrogen is therefore not marginal — it is systemic.

For emerging and developing economies, this transition represents a strategic development opportunity.

Hard-to-electrify sectors such as steel, chemicals, refining, shipping and aviation will require energy-dense, low-carbon fuels. If designed well, green hydrogen can reduce exposure to fossil fuel volatility, strengthen energy security, create skilled jobs and anchor new industrial value chains —when guided by strong governance and development-focused strategies.

Our report identifies three priorities to ensure green hydrogen supports equitable development:

⚖️ Build strategic foundations before committing to scale
With global hydrogen demand still dominated by fossil-based supply and costs for low-emissions hydrogen remaining 2–4 times higher in many regions, countries should prioritize phased pilots. Strategic demonstration projects allow learning, cost discovery, and institutional strengthening without creating fiscal or technological lock-in.

🔗 Integrate green hydrogen into broader industrial policy
Hydrogen should not be treated as a standalone sector. It must be embedded in coordinated energy planning, renewable capacity expansion, infrastructure development, skills strategies, and industrial upgrading. Given that hydrogen production requires large volumes of additional renewable electricity, system-level planning is essential to avoid diverting clean power away from households and productive sectors.

💰 De-risk strategically with governance safeguards
Blended finance, carbon contracts for difference, and public guarantees can help close viability gaps and crowd in private capital. But de-risking must be conditional on environmental safeguards, renewable additionality, water sustainability, local job creation, and transparent revenue frameworks to ensure that hydrogen projects contribute to long-term development outcomes.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these principles into practical strategies—supporting hydrogen roadmaps, identifying bankable projects, and aligning development with jobs, skills, environmental safeguards, and local industrial priorities.

For sectors where direct electrification is not feasible, green hydrogen can provide a pathway toward net-zero when aligned with inclusive development goals.

Energy has been centre stage at #Davos this week. And, amid all of this: AI. AI is not artificial. It has a long tail of energy-hungry physical data centres and GPU racks, critical mineral mining, and real-world inference demanding unprecedented power supplies.

So, how do we harness these two seemingly separate but, in reality, interconnected and intertwined revolutions - the energy transition, and the AI era? This is the focus of our new Bulletin, below, where we define the ‘digital energy stack’.

In the tech world, a ’stack’ is the collection of different technologies and components needed for a digital product or service to function. As you read this post, it sits on a ’stack’ of solutions: a web browser or LinkedIn application on your phone or other device. Internet and email protocols that (hopefully!) are displaying the below graphic and link correctly. And, layers of cloud hosting, connectivity, and - of course - energy, to make all of this happen.

We are applying this ‘stack’ approach to sustainable energy. We need a systems-level approach, and coherent and strategic efforts. There are seven elements in the ’digital energy stack’:

📊 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 - the 'fuel' of the energy revolution. Big, Lean, and Thick Data.
📱 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 - including 3G and 4G, and IoT.
🖥️ 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐞 - the 'currency' of the 21st century.
🪪 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 - to amplify the impact of inclusive energy.
🔒 𝐂𝐲𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 - recognising energy's status as critical national infrastructure. 
🤖 𝐀𝐈 - with AI driving new energy solutions, but also creating new challenges.
🏛️ 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 - shaping the talent, culture, and  institutions of the energy transition.

Importantly, there is no single pathway for any of these seven components. Digital and energy innovation is occurring and emerging everywhere, from Silicon Valley to the Silicon Savannah. The Global South is not just an innovation taker - but a maker, and shaper.

Without intentional design, digital risks reinforcing and entrenching energy inequality rather than accelerating an inclusive and just energy transition. The question is no longer whether AI and energy will intersect. It is whether we design that intersection to deliver development, resilience, and equity at scale.

🤝 Strengthening collaboration across energy, finance, digital, and governance systems

Global electricity demand is projected to grow by 3.6% annually between 2026 and 2030, driven by industry, electric mobility, cooling and data centres. Emerging economies will account for nearly 80% of additional demand, placing the Global South at the centre of this transformation.

At the same time, renewables are set to overtake coal, with renewables and nuclear reaching 50% of global generation by 2030, up from 42% today, while solar and wind rise from 17% to 27%. This shift creates a historic opportunity to align energy expansion with development and industrial transformation.

This is precisely the conversation unfolding at the International Energy Agency (IEA)  Ministerial 2026—where energy is central to geopolitical stability, economic competitiveness and global cooperation.

Yet affordability remains a critical constraint, as electricity prices in many countries have risen faster than incomes since 2019. The pathway forward lies in designing power systems that deliver efficiency across demand, supply and infrastructure use—through smart grids, regional interconnections, demand-side management, and blended finance mechanisms that crowd in private capital while protecting vulnerable households.

Unlocking these opportunities requires three interconnected solutions:

🔌 Scale grids and storage at speed
Annual grid investment must increase by roughly 50% from today’s USD 400 billion, combined with accelerated deployment of utility-scale batteries to enhance flexibility and energy security.

🌍 Develop integrated, development-focused energy systems
Combining grid expansion, distributed renewables, storage and digital system management can support electrification of transport, industry and communities while reducing import dependence.

💰 Ensure affordability and financial sustainability
Smart market design, demand-side efficiency, regional interconnections and blended finance mechanisms can crowd in private capital, protect vulnerable households and stabilise prices.

With global power sector emissions plateauing through 2030, the just energy transition is no longer a future aspiration—it is a present reality. The Global South is already demonstrating leadership in renewable expansion and system innovation, proving that development and decarbonisation can advance together, and setting the pace for a more resilient and inclusive global energy system.

#EnergyForDevelopment #IEAMinisterial

Can countries expand power systems without deepening energy poverty?

Global electricity demand is projected to grow by around 3.6% annually through 2030, driven by electrification of industry, cooling, transport, and digital services. As countries expand grids and generation capacity to meet rising demand, the scale of investment required is substantial.

Yet this expansion coincides with a persistent access and affordability gap. While around 92% of the global population had basic electricity access in 2023, 666 million people still remained without electricity, with the access gap heavily concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa.

But this moment is not only a development challenge — it is a strategic opportunity.
The acceleration of electricity demand can unlock new models of partnership, mobilize private capital at scale, and align infrastructure expansion with inclusive growth. With the right policy signals, regulatory clarity, and risk-mitigation instruments, private sector engagement can help close the financing gap while advancing affordability and equity.
Three approaches highlighted in UNDP’s From Commitments to Megawatts bulletin stand out:

💰 Implement targeted subsidies and financial mechanisms
Affordability remains a major barrier. UNDP analysis shows that only 22% of households without electricity can afford basic solar kits without support. Targeted subsidies can significantly expand uptake. In Togo, reducing PAYGo solar costs by 18–42% led to a 122% increase in adoption, with the strongest gains in underserved communities.

🔌 Scale decentralized renewable energy
Off-grid solar and mini-grids remain among the most cost-effective pathways to reach remote populations. These solutions have already provided electricity to over 560 million people globally, with the potential to reach nearly 400 million more by 2030 at lower cost than grid extension.

📊 Leverage data-driven energy planning
Data-driven tools such as least-cost power development planning enable governments to expand grids while prioritizing areas with the largest affordability and reliability gaps—ensuring that investments strengthen both capacity and inclusion.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these approaches into practical strategies—supporting integrated energy planning, financial de-risking, tariff reform, and decentralized renewable deployment that aligns infrastructure expansion with inclusive and sustainable development.

As electricity demand accelerates, the question is not only how fast systems grow—but whether expansion ensures affordability and equity.

Can countries double energy efficiency while electricity demand accelerates?

With electricity demand expected to grow 3.6% annually through 2030, driven by digitalization, AI, cooling, and electrification, efficiency is one of the fastest ways to reduce energy system costs. Global efficiency-related investment is set to reach almost USD 800 billion in 2025, over 70% since 2015.

The UAE Consensus commits countries to tripling renewables and doubling efficiency improvement rates to around 4% annually by 2030. Yet gains were only 1% in 2024 and are projected to reach just 1.8% in 2025.

Efficiency is an opportunity for the Global South. It reduces exposure to volatile electricity prices and has already avoided the need for 20% more fossil fuel imports. 

Since 2000, efficiency improvements have cut household energy bills in advanced economies by up to 20%, while industries now produce 20% more value per unit of energy than in 2000. 

Three coordinated areas can accelerate energy efficiency implementation solutions:

⚡ Strengthen national efficiency frameworks
Embedding efficiency targets into digital, industrial, and affordability policies is critical to reach the required 4% annual improvement rate. Brazil’s Artificial Intelligence Plan allocates over $900 million to support sustainable energy systems for data centers and AI infrastructure, demonstrating how digital strategies can align with national efficiency and decarbonization pathways.

💻 Reduce cooling demand for datacenters and digital infrastructure intensity 
Cooling systems account for between 7% of total electricity consumption in highly efficient hyperscale data centres and over 30% in less-efficient enterprise facilities.

📊 Deploy AI for system-wide optimization
AI can map infrastructure gaps, anticipate demand, and optimize energy flows in real time. AI is estimated to contribute up to 5.4 GtCO2e in annual emissions reductions by 2035 through accelerating low-carbon transitions across sectors.

UNDP  is supporting countries in aligning digital transformation with energy efficiency—integrating governance frameworks, smart infrastructure, and system optimization with sustainable development goals.

Can countries expand power systems without deepening energy poverty?

Global electricity demand is projected to grow by around 3.6% annually through 2030, driven by electrification of industry, cooling, transport, and digital services. As countries expand grids and generation capacity to meet rising demand, the scale of investment required is substantial.

Yet this expansion coincides with a persistent access and affordability gap. While around 92% of the global population had basic electricity access in 2023, 666 million people still remained without electricity, with the access gap heavily concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa.

But this moment is not only a development challenge — it is a strategic opportunity.
The acceleration of electricity demand can unlock new models of partnership, mobilize private capital at scale, and align infrastructure expansion with inclusive growth. With the right policy signals, regulatory clarity, and risk-mitigation instruments, private sector engagement can help close the financing gap while advancing affordability and equity.
Three approaches highlighted in UNDP’s From Commitments to Megawatts bulletin stand out:

💰 Implement targeted subsidies and financial mechanisms
Affordability remains a major barrier. UNDP analysis shows that only 22% of households without electricity can afford basic solar kits without support. Targeted subsidies can significantly expand uptake. In Togo, reducing PAYGo solar costs by 18–42% led to a 122% increase in adoption, with the strongest gains in underserved communities.

🔌 Scale decentralized renewable energy
Off-grid solar and mini-grids remain among the most cost-effective pathways to reach remote populations. These solutions have already provided electricity to over 560 million people globally, with the potential to reach nearly 400 million more by 2030 at lower cost than grid extension.

📊 Leverage data-driven energy planning
Data-driven tools such as least-cost power development planning enable governments to expand grids while prioritizing areas with the largest affordability and reliability gaps—ensuring that investments strengthen both capacity and inclusion.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these approaches into practical strategies—supporting integrated energy planning, financial de-risking, tariff reform, and decentralized renewable deployment that aligns infrastructure expansion with inclusive and sustainable development.

As electricity demand accelerates, the question is not only how fast systems grow—but whether expansion ensures affordability and equity.

Everyone loves handing out/receiving carrots in climate and green industrial policy, but few politicians want to talk about the sticks, which are more politically sensitive.

A new important paper in Nature by Wei Peng, Jonas Meckling, Huilin Luo, Allen Fawcett, Jonas Nahm Jessica F. Green, Gokul Iyer, & David G. Victor explores what happens to decarbonisation when we sequence carrots (e.g. green subsidies) and sticks (carbon taxes).

They find that carrots alone (without shifting to sticks) does not achieve deep decarbonization by mid-century, and you still need almost the same size sticks later anyway. In other words, sequencing matters but cannot substitute for the presence and quality of sticks. Delaying hard policies does not necessarily avoids them; it may just postpones them, potentially at higher cost.

The next question: what types of sticks are more likely to be effective than others, under what conditions and for different objectives, such as green industrial capability accumulation in developing nations?

How can countries leverage green hydrogen to decarbonize hard-to-electrify industries while strengthening development outcomes?

Global hydrogen demand reached 100 million tonnes (Mt) in 2024, growing by nearly 2% from 2023, in line with overall energy demand growth. Yet it is still produced almost entirely from fossil fuels, consuming around 290 billion cubic metres of natural gas and 90 million tonnes of coal equivalent each year. The transition to low-emissions hydrogen is therefore not marginal — it is systemic.

For emerging and developing economies, this transition represents a strategic development opportunity.

Hard-to-electrify sectors such as steel, chemicals, refining, shipping and aviation will require energy-dense, low-carbon fuels. If designed well, green hydrogen can reduce exposure to fossil fuel volatility, strengthen energy security, create skilled jobs and anchor new industrial value chains —when guided by strong governance and development-focused strategies.

Our report identifies three priorities to ensure green hydrogen supports equitable development:

⚖️ Build strategic foundations before committing to scale
With global hydrogen demand still dominated by fossil-based supply and costs for low-emissions hydrogen remaining 2–4 times higher in many regions, countries should prioritize phased pilots. Strategic demonstration projects allow learning, cost discovery, and institutional strengthening without creating fiscal or technological lock-in.

🔗 Integrate green hydrogen into broader industrial policy
Hydrogen should not be treated as a standalone sector. It must be embedded in coordinated energy planning, renewable capacity expansion, infrastructure development, skills strategies, and industrial upgrading. Given that hydrogen production requires large volumes of additional renewable electricity, system-level planning is essential to avoid diverting clean power away from households and productive sectors.

💰 De-risk strategically with governance safeguards
Blended finance, carbon contracts for difference, and public guarantees can help close viability gaps and crowd in private capital. But de-risking must be conditional on environmental safeguards, renewable additionality, water sustainability, local job creation, and transparent revenue frameworks to ensure that hydrogen projects contribute to long-term development outcomes.

UNDP is working with countries to translate these principles into practical strategies—supporting hydrogen roadmaps, identifying bankable projects, and aligning development with jobs, skills, environmental safeguards, and local industrial priorities.

For sectors where direct electrification is not feasible, green hydrogen can provide a pathway toward net-zero when aligned with inclusive development goals.

Green hydrogen could supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050. Yet today, less than 1% of production is low-carbon, and much of the investment remains concentrated away from many of the Global South’s lowest-cost production regions.

The question is not only whether green hydrogen can scale, but whether it will strengthen national development and improve people’s lives, or primarily serve external energy demand.

For countries in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East, green hydrogen offers real opportunities: supporting industrial development, creating jobs, strengthening energy security, and diversifying economies. Some estimates suggest that hydrogen-related value chains could generate hundreds of thousands of jobs in emerging markets if local industries and skills are developed. But without careful planning, it risks repeating extractive models where resources are exported while local value creation remains limited.

Producing 1 kg of green hydrogen can require around 9 liters of purified water, meaning that large-scale projects may demand millions of cubic meters of water in regions that are already water-stressed. Land requirements are also significant: producing 1 million tons of hydrogen can require around 30,000 hectares of solar capacity, raising important questions about land use and ecosystem protection.

This is why UNDP , together with the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, developed the 3P framework — People, Planet, and Prosperity. The framework helps ensure that hydrogen strategies align with national development priorities, operate within ecological limits, and generate shared economic benefits.

Green hydrogen is often labelled the “fuel of the future,” projected to meet up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050. But can this transition also become an opportunity the Global South?

Today at the European Hydrogen Energy Conference (EHEC) , I discussed how green hydrogen could help reduce fossil fuel dependence and strengthen energy security. Yet nearly 99% of hydrogen production still relies on fossil fuels.

The EU Industrial Accelerator Act offers an important reference for boosting local industry, jobs, and clean technologies. However, hydrogen investment remains highly concentrated: 83% of global investments are located in Europe and China, highlighting the challenges many emerging economies face in attracting investment and building domestic hydrogen industries.

Green hydrogen could be a pivotal opportunity for the Global South to decarbonize industrial sectors, but the key question is how to scale this opportunity in ways that deliver real benefits for people, the planet, and long-term economic growth.

1. Green hydrogen should strengthen human capital and energy systems.
For many countries in the Global South, hydrogen offers an opportunity to diversify economies and capture first-mover advantages in emerging clean industries. With abundant solar and wind resources, production costs could reach $1.15–$1.74/kg by 2050, compared with $2.8–$4+ in many Global North countries.

2. Expansion must operate within environmental limits.
Around 70% of planned electrolyser capacity is located in water-stressed regions. Energy security cannot come at the expense of water security and ecosystem protection.

3. Financing green hydrogen must generate inclusive growth.
Many of the world’s lowest-cost hydrogen production sites still face renewable financing costs 24–32% higher than in the Global North, limiting their ability to scale.

Diversification can strengthen energy security — but not on its own. Turning green hydrogen’s potential into real progress requires policies that translate this opportunity into local jobs, resilient energy systems, and sustainable economic development.

Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Artificial intelligence is advancing at an extraordinary pace — opening a frontier that demands both imagination and responsibility. On one hand, AI holds immense potential to reshape our world. On the other, Earth’s life-support systems — climate, biodiversity, and water — are under unprecedented strain, and meeting these challenges will require ever more energy.

Global energy demand grew by 2.2% in 2024 — nearly double the recent decade’s average — with electricity consumption jumping by 4.3% as electrification, heat waves, data centers, and digitalization surged. Over the 2025–2027 period, electricity demand is expected to keep rising at around 3.9% annually.

In 2024, AI consumed 415 TWh of electricity — more than 150 individual countries. By 2030, global data center demand could reach 945 TWh, exceeding Japan’s total electricity use. Meanwhile, 1.18 billion people still live without reliable access to energy.

This poses an important question: what kind of intelligence are we building? Can AI learn from nature to design future energy systems that deliver a just transition?

In a reflection co-authored with Riad Meddeb , we explore the idea of Planetary Intelligence — the integration of human, technological, and natural systems to sustain habitable conditions.

Synchronize energy with the planet’s balance - AI can move beyond optimizing data centers to orchestrate energy flows as nature does — cutting grid losses, balancing renewables in real time, reducing emissions by up to 10% by 2030, and unlocking 175 GW of additional transmission capacity.

Integrating planetary health into our energy systems for smarter societies - When designed to mirror natural systems, AI can help manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity — generating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while preserving the ecosystems that sustain life.

Advancing an inclusive and equitable energy future -  From tracking bird migrations around wind farms to developing over 40 African language models, AI can amplify diverse voices and ensure that the energy transition becomes not only smarter — but also fairer and more resilient.

If AI is trained on the principles that govern life on Earth, it can help us see both the forest and the trees — guiding us toward an energy future that is more intelligent, more just, and more human.

Read more about planetary intelligence in our recent publication on Illuminem: https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB

UN Environment Programme’s State of Finance for Nature Report 2026 shows that significantly more financial resources are spent on degrading nature than conserving it. For example, for every US$1 invested in protecting nature, US$30 are spent destroying it.

Many of these potentially harmful financial flows are linked to incentives and subsidies across sectors such as agriculture, fisheries and energy.

Target 18 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework calls for identifying and eliminating, phasing out or reforming incentives, including subsidies, that are harmful to biodiversity, while scaling up positive incentives for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity.

Addressing these incentives is an important step toward aligning financial flows with the goals of the Global Biodiversity Framework.

Are we paying trillions to avoid investing billions? 
  
Today, 2.1 billion people, about one in four globally, still cook with polluting fuels. In sub-Saharan Africa, only 7% of rural households have access to clean cooking. 
  
The economics are just as stark. Dirty cooking costs the global economy an estimated $2.4 to $4 trillion each year through health impacts, environmental damage, and lost productivity. Yet global investment in clean cooking remains around $2.5 billion annually, less than a third of what is needed. 
  
That is not just a funding gap. It is a priorities gap. 
  
Clean cooking is still seen only as a household issue, when in reality it sits at the intersection of health, development, gender equality, and economic productivity. 
  
It reflects a whole-of-system value chain and national ecosystem, from energy planning and fuel supply chains to financing, data systems, and last-mile delivery, that treats clean cooking as essential infrastructure, not an afterthought. 
  
Three shifts are especially important: 
  
1️⃣ Integrate clean cooking into national energy planning 
Clean cooking cannot remain siloed. Embedding it in electrification strategies, renewable energy deployment, and broader energy access planning can help solutions reach more people, faster and more sustainably. 
  
2️⃣ Design financing that reaches rural and low-income households 
Upfront costs remain the biggest barrier for the households that need clean cooking most. Grants, subsidies, and innovative financing models are essential where market forces alone will not deliver. 
  
3️⃣ Use digital tools to improve targeting and efficiency 
Demand mapping, spatial planning, remote monitoring, and results-based financing can help make clean cooking programmes more effective, affordable, and scalable. 
 
In a world building artificial intelligence, smart grids, and autonomous vehicles, we cannot afford to leave a quarter of the world’s population without access to clean cooking.  
 
The technologies exist. The solutions are known. What is needed now is sustained commitment and investment to translate solutions into real change for each of the 2.1 billion people who still lack access to clean cooking. 
  
#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanCooking #SDG7

Across the region, we are witnessing ongoing attacks and devastating human loss. And as the situation continues to escalate, its implications for global energy flows will shape the years to come. Recent attacks on Iranian gas facilities have already driven oil prices upward, with fears of further disruptions to infrastructure across the Gulf and key export routes.

While this is felt most immediately in the region, these shocks do not stay contained. They ripple through global energy systems, affecting prices, supply, and stability, reinforcing the need to phase out fossil fuels and expand the energy transition.

In moments like these, energy becomes very immediate, determining whether people can keep the lights on, afford fuel, or cook a meal at the end of the day. We’ve seen this before. During the 2022 global energy crisis, rising fuel prices threatened to push an estimated 100 million people back toward polluting cooking fuels, reversing years of progress. In many parts of Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia, where access is already fragile, households were among the first to absorb these shocks.

Clean cooking sits within this broader reality. It’s not separate from the conversations we’re having today around energy, crisis, and uncertainty. Access to something as basic as cooking is often one of the first things to shift when conditions deteriorate.

I’ve been thinking a lot about this through conversations with colleagues at UNDP working on energy justice. How the ongoing atrocities don’t just affect one country or one region, but are part of a larger, interconnected system. From whether households can afford to cook, to how countries respond to shifting energy supplies, to what this means for the future of renewables and the critical minerals behind them.

Can the energy transition become the largest development investment opportunity of this decade?

We are entering a new phase of the global energy transition. The question is no longer whether it is happening, but whether our systems, our finance, and our institutions are moving fast enough to keep up with development realities. 

Energy is now at the centre of economic resilience and national security, making diversification of clean energy mixes a key opportunity to strengthen resilience in the context of rising geopolitical tensions. In 2024, investment in clean energy technologies reached USD 2.4 trillion. 
Demand for critical minerals could triple by 2030. Electricity demand is expected to grow more than 50 percent faster in the next decade than in the previous one, driven by electrification, cooling, and the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure—
But development realities are moving even faster. Regions where demand is growing fastest still receive a fraction of global investment.

This is exactly why, as @UN energy  partners, we bring together policy, finance, technology, and development efforts across the UN system and beyond, to move from fragmented actions to a coordinated, system-wide response—linking energy access, clean cooking, and just transition pathways.

UN-Energy connects expertise across energy, health, food, education, industry, finance, and digital to deliver at scale, responding to this new phase of the energy transition that requires integrated, interconnected solutions.

This week, I will be in Geneva for the #SDG7 Expert Group Meeting, convened by @UN DESA and hosted by UNECE - United Nations Economic Commission for Europe . The discussions will help shape the policy conversations leading into the HLPF and identify practical ways to accelerate progress on energy access and energy transitions, including clean cooking and resilient, diversified energy systems.

Looking forward to engaging with colleagues and partners in Geneva on how we can deliver a final push toward SDG7.
#SDG7 #EnergyforDevelopment #SustainableDevelopment #UNEnergy
